steps.label: THE PREDICTION
steps.title: Could an app predict you surprisingly well?
steps.lead: Make the bet before we explain anything.
steps.studentTask: Choose one answer silently on your own. Do not discuss it yet. After you submit, look up.
steps.roomInstruction: Choose silently on your own. Commit your answer, then look up. We will return to this prediction at the end.
steps.afterSubmit: Your prediction is locked in. Keep it to yourself for now and look up.
choices: PROVE IT — an app could predict me pretty well
NO CHANCE — it would get important things about me wrong

runbook.setup: Give students 20 seconds of silence. Tell them not to discuss their answer.
runbook.say: Before I explain anything, make a bet: could the apps you use every day predict you surprisingly well, or would they get the important parts of you wrong?
runbook.studentDoes: Students choose independently and submit one answer.
runbook.askNext: Do not ask for explanations yet. Preserve the mystery.
runbook.watchFor: Students trying to discuss before committing.
runbook.advanceWhen: About 80–90% of active students have committed.
runbook.ifStuck: Name TikTok, Spotify, Netflix, YouTube, or Amazon as familiar prediction systems.
runbook.transition: Keep your answer. We are coming back to it.

steps.label: DIGITAL SHADOW
steps.title: You watched three videos about running shoes.
steps.lead: What does the system actually know?
steps.studentTask: Choose the ONE statement the platform directly observed. Ask yourself: what did it see, and what are we merely inferring?
steps.roomInstruction: OBSERVED or INFERRED? Choose the one thing the platform actually knows from the evidence given.

teachReveal.headline: DATA ≠ MEANING
teachReveal.explanation: The system observed three video views. Liking running, needing shoes, and being a runner are interpretations built from that trace.

runbook.setup: Read the scenario exactly as written. Do not hint that this is about inference.
runbook.say: You watched three videos about running shoes. Which of these things does the platform actually know?
runbook.watchFor: Students confidently treating identity or intent as observed fact.
runbook.askNext: Which of these things did the platform literally observe? Did it ever see you run?
runbook.teachableMoment: Let incorrect answers remain visible for a beat. The mistake is the lesson: behavioral traces invite us to turn inference into fact.
runbook.landHere: DATA ≠ MEANING. Observation and interpretation are different layers.
runbook.ifStuck: Cross out each statement the platform could not directly observe.
runbook.advanceWhen: Students can explain why only the video views are directly observed.
runbook.transition: AI begins with clues. What happens when those clues move through a system?

steps.label: TEACH THE SYSTEM
steps.title: AI is not magic. It is a system.
steps.lead: Phones down. Trace a recommendation through five parts.
steps.studentTask: Put your phone down and look up. Follow one familiar recommendation from the data collected to the action a person takes.
steps.roomInstruction: PHONES DOWN. Follow the chain: DATA → MODEL / TOOL → OUTPUT → HUMAN INTERPRETATION → DECISION / ACTION.
flow: DECISION / ACTION — click, buy, watch, share

runbook.setup: Shift attention completely away from devices. Point to each layer as you teach it.
runbook.say: AI feels mysterious when we look only at the output. Slow it down and it becomes a system we can inspect.
runbook.studentDoes: Students listen and help trace Spotify, TikTok, or Netflix through the five layers aloud.
runbook.askNext: Where does the AI end and the human decision begin? At what point can a recommendation become consequential?
runbook.watchFor: Students collapsing MODEL / TOOL and OUTPUT into the same thing.
runbook.teachableMoment: Use Spotify: songs played are data; the recommendation logic is the model; Discover Weekly is an output; deciding it knows your taste is interpretation; pressing play is action.
runbook.landHere: AI output is one part of a larger human decision system.
runbook.ifStuck: Trace Spotify end-to-end before asking students for another example.
runbook.advanceWhen: The class can verbally trace one example through all five layers.
runbook.transition: Now you are going to become the model.

steps.label: BE THE ALGORITHM
steps.title: Which three clues should Viking Feed trust most?
steps.lead: Talk with your group first. Choose only three.
steps.studentTask: Form a group of 2–3. Discuss all eight clues. Agree on the THREE signals your group would trust most. One person submits for the group. Be ready to defend one choice.
steps.roomInstruction: GROUPS OF 2–3. Choose exactly 3 signals to trust. One person submits. Be ready to defend a choice and name an assumption.
steps.afterSubmit: Your group's three signals are in. Keep discussing: which choice was hardest to agree on?

runbook.setup: Say: get into groups of 2–3. One device submits, but every person must contribute to the decision.
runbook.say: You are Viking Feed. You have eight clues about Maya, but you can only trust three. Decide which three deserve the most influence.
runbook.studentDoes: Groups discuss the signals, select exactly three, and prepare to defend one choice.
runbook.watchFor: Gaming club once = gamer; pizza twice = loves pizza; late-night activity = prefers nightlife.
runbook.askNext: Which clue caused the most disagreement? What assumption did your group make about Maya? Which clue would you throw away first?
runbook.teachableMoment: Feature selection is already a judgment. The algorithm has not predicted anything yet, but human assumptions are already shaping what it will see.
runbook.landHere: Choosing what data matters is itself a consequential design decision.
runbook.ifStuck: Ask groups to eliminate five signals instead of choosing three.
runbook.advanceWhen: Most groups have submitted and you have heard at least two different rationales.
runbook.transition: Your model has evidence. Now it has to ship an output.

steps.label: SHIP THE OUTPUT
steps.title: What should Viking Feed recommend to Maya?
steps.studentTask: Work independently again. Based only on the information you have so far, choose the recommendation Viking Feed should send Maya.
steps.roomInstruction: INDEPENDENT DECISION. No discussion. Choose the recommendation Viking Feed should ship based only on what it knows now.

runbook.setup: Break the group conversation. Tell everyone this vote is individual.
runbook.say: Your system has to ship. Based only on what Viking Feed knows right now, what should it recommend?
runbook.studentDoes: Every student commits one recommendation independently.
runbook.watchFor: Students looking to peers before answering.
runbook.landHere: A system eventually turns uncertain evidence into an output.
runbook.ifStuck: Remind them that Not enough information is a legitimate system output.
runbook.advanceWhen: At least 85% of active students have committed.
runbook.transition: Now we can audit what our algorithm produced.

steps.label: REVEAL + DEBATE
steps.title: The class has spoken. Defend the minority.
steps.lead: Phones down. The winning answer is less interesting than the reasoning.
steps.studentTask: Put your phone down. Listen to the class result. Find reasoning you disagree with and be ready to explain what evidence supports your view.
steps.roomInstruction: PHONES DOWN. Defend a minority answer. Then ask: What did we assume that Maya's data never actually told us?
teachableMoments: Gaming club once does not equal gamer.
Two pizza orders do not equal pizza preference.
Following classmates does not prove extroversion.
Late-night activity does not tell us why Maya was awake.

runbook.setup: Reveal the distribution, then stop talking for three seconds so students can take in the split.
runbook.say: The winning answer is less interesting than why we produced it. Someone defend one of the least popular choices.
runbook.studentDoes: Students discuss the evidence behind different recommendations and identify hidden assumptions.
runbook.watchFor: Correlation becoming certainty; a single behavior becoming identity.
runbook.askNext: What did we infer that Maya's profile never actually said? What would we need to know before trusting our recommendation?
runbook.teachableMoment: Use the actual room split. Do not reward the majority simply for being the majority.
runbook.landHere: DATA ≠ MEANING. The same evidence can support different interpretations.
runbook.ifStuck: Ask: does attending gaming club once make someone a gamer?
runbook.advanceWhen: Students identify at least three assumptions embedded in the recommendations.
runbook.transition: Now I am going to change the context without changing the algorithm.

steps.label: THE PLOT TWIST
steps.title: Same Maya. New context.
steps.lead: Do not vote yet. Notice when your thinking moves.
steps.studentTask: Do not submit anything. Look up. Your instructor will reveal three new facts one at a time. After each one, notice what changed in your interpretation.
steps.roomInstruction: DO NOT VOTE YET. Three new facts are coming. After each reveal, ask yourself: what assumption just changed?

reveals.text: Gaming club happened because Maya's roommate asked her to go.
reveals.question: What assumption weakened?

reveals.text: Maya has been looking for ways to meet people outside her residence hall.
reveals.question: What became more plausible?

reveals.text: Maya has a major exam at 8 AM tomorrow.
reveals.question: Which old signals matter less?

runbook.setup: Reveal each fact slowly. Leave a few seconds between facts; do not race through all three.
runbook.say: Do not vote. I want you to notice the exact moment your recommendation starts to move.
runbook.studentDoes: Students watch each reveal, discuss what it changes, and hold their new recommendation privately.
runbook.watchFor: Students recognizing that none of the historical behavioral data changed.
runbook.askNext: After each fact: what assumption weakened? Which signal just became less useful?
runbook.teachableMoment: Context changes the meaning of existing data without changing the raw data itself.
runbook.landHere: More data is not always the answer. Sometimes the missing ingredient is context.
runbook.ifStuck: Ask which new fact has the highest decision value and why.
runbook.advanceWhen: All three context changes have been discussed.
runbook.transition: Now commit again using the better context.

steps.label: VOTE AGAIN
steps.title: What should Viking Feed recommend now?
steps.studentTask: Choose independently again. It is okay to change your answer. Commit the recommendation you would make with the new context.
steps.roomInstruction: VOTE AGAIN. Same system, better context. Changing your mind is evidence of updating, not failure.

runbook.setup: Explicitly normalize changing an answer before students vote.
runbook.say: Changing your mind is not failure. It is what good reasoning looks like when better information arrives.
runbook.studentDoes: Students independently submit a second recommendation.
runbook.watchFor: Students holding the old answer merely to remain consistent.
runbook.askNext: Which new fact had the most influence on your second decision?
runbook.landHere: Responsible decisions should update when relevant evidence changes.
runbook.advanceWhen: Most first-round voters have voted again.
runbook.transition: Now watch what happened to the room.

steps.label: SHIFT
steps.title: The room moved.
steps.lead: Watch what happened when context changed.
steps.studentTask: Look up. Compare the class before and after. Be ready to explain what changed in the five-part system.
steps.roomInstruction: LOOK UP. How many people changed their minds? What changed: the algorithm, the data, the interpretation, or the decision?
steps.hero: The algorithm didn't change. The information did.

runbook.setup: Pause on the Shift visualization. Do not immediately explain it for them.
runbook.say: This number matters more than the winning answer: how many people moved when relevant context changed.
runbook.studentDoes: Students interpret the before/after movement and connect it to the five-part framework.
runbook.watchFor: The misconception that the model itself became smarter.
runbook.askNext: What actually changed across our five-part system? Why did that change the decision?
runbook.teachableMoment: Make changing one's mind visible as intellectual progress rather than error.
runbook.landHere: The algorithm did not change. The information and human interpretation did.
runbook.ifStuck: Trace one student's possible before-and-after reasoning path.
runbook.advanceWhen: Students can explain the shift using the framework.
runbook.transition: Context helped our system. Now let's see all the places it can fail.

steps.label: BREAK THE ALGORITHM
steps.title: Where can the failure enter?
steps.lead: More than one answer can be defensible.
steps.studentTask: Choose the point in the five-part system you think creates the greatest risk. Then prepare to defend why another point could also cause failure.
steps.roomInstruction: DIAGNOSE THE FAILURE. Choose the greatest risk, then be ready to defend a different layer too. There is no single correct answer.
choices: DATA — missing, wrong, or biased information
MODEL / TOOL — bad patterns or wrong objective

runbook.setup: Tell students explicitly that this is a diagnosis, not a trivia question.
runbook.say: We often say an AI failed as though failure lives in one place. Where in this whole system could harm enter?
runbook.studentDoes: Students choose a risk point and then discuss how failure can propagate across layers.
runbook.watchFor: Students selecting MODEL / TOOL only because it sounds most technical.
runbook.askNext: Can someone defend a different layer? Could two layers fail at once?
runbook.teachableMoment: Responsible AI is not only model quality. Data, outputs, interpretation, and action all matter.
runbook.landHere: AI responsibility belongs to the whole sociotechnical system.
runbook.ifStuck: Give one concrete failure example for each layer.
runbook.advanceWhen: At least two different failure points have been convincingly defended.
runbook.transition: One final way outputs can mislead us: confidence-looking numbers.

steps.label: 97% MATCH
steps.title: 97% MATCH
steps.studentTask: React first. Would a 97% MATCH make you more likely to trust the recommendation? Choose one answer before we unpack the number.
steps.roomInstruction: 97% MATCH. Would you trust it? Vote first. Then ask the question the number is trying to make you forget.
choices: No — the number tells me almost nothing

teachReveal.headline: 97% match with what?
teachReveal.explanation: Precision can create authority without telling you what was measured, how reliable it is, or whether the decision is appropriate.

runbook.setup: Let the giant 97% dominate the Room before giving any explanation.
runbook.say: Do not overthink it. Viking Feed says 97% MATCH. Does that make the recommendation more trustworthy?
runbook.studentDoes: Students vote, then interrogate what the percentage actually represents.
runbook.watchFor: Precision being mistaken for validity or confidence being mistaken for correctness.
runbook.askNext: 97% of what? Compared with whom? Measured how? Does a confident prediction make a good decision?
runbook.teachableMoment: The visual authority of the number is part of the lesson. Let students feel its persuasive pull first.
runbook.landHere: A precise-looking output is not automatically a meaningful or trustworthy output.
runbook.ifStuck: Ask what information they would need before the 97% became useful.
runbook.advanceWhen: Students begin questioning the metric rather than merely reacting to its size.
runbook.transition: Return to the bet you made at the very beginning.

steps.label: CALLBACK
steps.title: Would you make the same bet now?
steps.studentTask: Return to your opening prediction and vote again. You may choose the same answer, but your reason should now be stronger and more precise.
steps.roomInstruction: CALLBACK. Return to your opening bet. Would you answer the same way now? Same answer is okay; better reasoning is the goal.
choices: PROVE IT — AI can predict patterns in my behavior
NO CHANCE — prediction is not the same as understanding me

runbook.setup: Remind students that the goal is not to force a changed answer.
runbook.say: I am not looking for everyone to switch sides. I am looking for a better reason than you had 75 minutes ago.
runbook.studentDoes: Students vote again and compare their reasoning with the opening prediction.
runbook.watchFor: Nuance: useful behavioral prediction can exist without genuine understanding of a person.
runbook.askNext: Is predicting what someone clicks the same as understanding who they are? What can prediction do well, and what can it miss?
runbook.teachableMoment: A sophisticated answer can be either side. Reward reasoning, not convergence.
runbook.landHere: Prediction is not the same as understanding.
runbook.ifStuck: Ask whether Spotify can predict your next song without understanding you as a person.
runbook.advanceWhen: The room has committed its second prediction and articulated the distinction.
runbook.transition: One sentence will capture what changed in your thinking.

steps.label: EXIT
steps.title: Finish one sentence.
steps.lead: Before today, I thought AI prediction was… Now I think… because…
steps.studentTask: Write ONE sentence that shows how your thinking changed or became more precise. Submit it before you leave.
steps.roomInstruction: EXIT: One sentence. Before today, I thought AI prediction was… Now I think… because…
steps.afterSubmit: Done. Thanks for thinking with the room today.
steps.placeholder: Before today… Now I think… because…

runbook.setup: Keep this brief. Students should be able to complete it as they pack up.
runbook.say: Give me one sentence that shows what changed or became more precise in your thinking.
runbook.studentDoes: Students write and submit one concise reflection.
runbook.watchFor: Evidence of observation vs inference, context, the five-part system, or prediction vs understanding.
runbook.askNext: No debrief needed unless time remains.
runbook.landHere: AI can support a decision. It does not remove human responsibility.
